chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Attar (may God be pleased with him) narrated from his father, from Muhammad ibn al-Hussein ibn Abi al-Khattab, from Ja'far ibn Bashir al-Bajli, from Abu Yahya Mu'amar al-Qattan, from Bashir al-Dahan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family), in the illness in which he died, said: 'Call my friend to me.' So they sent for his two fathers (Abu Bakr and Umar). When he looked at them, he turned his face away from them and said: 'Call my friend to me.' So Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him) was sent for. When he looked at him, he leaned over him and conversed with him. When he came out, the two men met him and asked: 'What did your friend tell you?' He said: 'He told me of a thousand gates, each gate opening a thousand gates.'

key_terms.أَبَوَيْهِمَا: His two fathers (referring to Abu Bakr and Umar, as they were the fathers of the wives Aisha and Hafsa)
key_terms.أَلْفَ بَابٍ: A thousand gates (metaphor for vast knowledge or authority)
key_terms.خَلِيلِي: My friend (referring to Ali ibn Abi Talib)
key_terms.يَفْتَحُ: Opens (indicating the expansive nature of the knowledge conveyed)

ai.seo_question: What did the Prophet Muhammad tell Ali ibn Abi Talib during his final illness?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Al-Khisal*, the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family) distinguishes Ali ibn Abi Talib as his true 'Khalil' (intimate friend) by engaging him in a private discourse during his final illness, contrasting this with the rejection of other companions. This exclusive communication underscores Ali’s unique spiritual station and his role as the inheritor of the Prophet’s esoteric knowledge (*‘Ilm al-Batin*). The metaphor of 'a thousand gates, each opening a thousand gates' highlights the infinite depth of divine wisdom transmitted through the Ahl al-Bayt, a concept central to Shia theological understanding of prophetic succession.
